10032870:
Home Care & Hospice Alliance of Maine Testimony on LD 210, the Governor's proposed Biennial Budget
February 12, 2025
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Appropriations & Financial Affairs Committee and Health & Human Services Committee:
My name is Sara Ratcliffe, and I serve as Executive Director of the Home Care and Hospice Alliance of Maine. The Alliance is submitting testimony in opposition to LD 210, the Governor's Biennial Budget proposal.
The Home Care and Hospice Alliance of Maine is a network of home care, hospice, and personal care providers across our State delivering in-home care to older adults and disabled individuals of all ages, allowing them to stay in their homes and communities.
While the Alliance recognizes that this was a difficult budget for the Administration to craft, we are deeply concerned about several issues in this proposal, specifically the lack of funding for MaineCare rate increases and cost-of-living adjustments and the proposed cut to the hospice rate.
Rates for Home & Community Based Services:
While we appreciate the proposed $122 million investment per year to stabilize the MaineCare program and cover current service levels, we are deeply troubled that this budget proposal does not contain any funding for MaineCare rate increases for home care services.
Providers of home care services have been vocal about the need for MaineCare rate increases for many years, especially for clinical services such as nursing. These services are a critical part of the healthcare continuum. Currently there are thousands of hours of unmet nursing care in the home care sector each month, and this is directly tied to inadequate reimbursement rates.
The Home Care & Hospice Alliance of Maine worked on legislation to raise rates during the 129th and 130th legislative sessions, but funding was not appropriated. During the 130th session, the Legislature worked with DHHS to enact a standard process for rate setting. Since that time, providers of home care services have been patiently awaiting their turn in the queue for a rate determination process. DHHS began the process of examining rates for home and community based services in 2024. According to DHHS, this rate determination process is scheduled to be completed in April of this year,

however no funding was included in this budget to cover rate increases for these services.
Current wages for nurses in home care have fallen drastically behind market rates due to low MaineCare reimbursement rates. Current reimbursement rates for these services are based off a 2016 rate study, which utilized data from 2012-2014. Utilizing date from 2012 to reimburse for services in 2025 is completely inadequate and has led to severe workforce shortages and care deserts across the state.
In fact, in testimony on the Alliance's 2021 bill to address this issue, DHHS acknowledged the insufficient rates for these services, stating that, "...Section 19 and 96 nursing rates are low and in need of an update, averaging only 52% of the comparison rate."
Home care agencies can't compete with other providers to hire enough nurses. For many of our member agencies, the patients they serve are almost entirely MaineCare patients. There are no other payers that can help pick up the slack from inadequate MaineCare rates. The result is that many patients are receiving far fewer hours of nursing services than what they need and are approved for. Others simply are not admitted to home care services due to the lack of staffing. Patients are having to leave their homes and go into hospitals and nursing homes because of the lack of nursing services - which is directly tied to low reimbursement rates.
Home care is a critical part of Maine's health care continuum. By caring for people at home, we keep them out of more costly settings like hospitals and nursing homes. The patients cared for in home-based settings are our most vulnerable - children with complex medical needs and older Mainers in need of care at home.
We urge you to include funding for MaineCare rate increases for home care services in this biennial budget.
MaineCare COLA adjustments for FY26-27:
According to current statute, DHHS was required to implement a cost-of-living adjustment for MaineCare services in January, but unfortunately these COLAs were not put into place. After years of stagnant rates, annual COLAs have been nothing short of a lifeline for Alliance members, their workforce, and the patients they care for. Many of our members crafted their annual budgets based on the knowledge that they would receive these COLA increases in January. Now they are left with significant deficits with no recourse for balancing their budgets.
In addition, this budget proposes changes to the MaineCare rate reform statutory language to stipulate that rate adjustments and COLAs are subject to available

appropriations. We are concerned about the precent this would set. What is the point of having a standardized rate setting process, if the determined rates are not actually implemented? There are always a multitude of competing priorities in the State budget and many other ways we could use our limited resources. However, if we have determined that setting and paying adequate rates for MaineCare services is a priority for our State, we should not enact language that opens such a gaping loophole for following through on that responsibility.
We urge you to seriously consider the need for this language change and the consequences it would lead to. In addition, we urge you to include funding for MaineCare COLAs in the biennial budget. While we understand that COLAs cannot be implemented retroactively, the department could act to implement the increases as soon as this budget passes.
Hospice rate change:
The budget proposal includes a funding cut to reflect rate changes for MaineCare Section 43, Hospice Services. The department is proposing cutting the hospice rate from 123% to 100% of the Medicare rate. Hospice providers were not expecting this cut and are concerned with the impact this cut would have on service delivery across the State.
We are also concerned that the department is proposing this change outside of the rate setting process laid out in statute. According to the department's proposed schedule for rate determinations, they are planning to initiate a rate determination process for MaineCare Section 43 in calendar year 2025. Instead of following the process laid out in statute and undertaking this rate determination first, the department is instead proposing a rate cut for hospice services in this budget without a comprehensive look at the rate or any feedback from providers. This appears to run completely counter to statutory requirements for rate setting.
In 2001, the legislature passed a law directing MaineCare to establish a hospice benefit and directed the department to establish reimbursement at the Medicare rate plus 23%. There was clear intent to reimburse hospice care at a level to cover the cost of providing care. Individuals accessing MaineCare hospice services are younger than Medicare beneficiaries with ages ranging from children to young adults. Younger individuals facing an end of life diagnosis often seek more aggressive care options to extend their life and palliative services to manage symptoms. Care for the family is also more complex as patients may be the parents of children or the patient may in fact be the child. End of life care for this population is different than caring for elderly individuals seeking comfort care at end of life.

Our understanding of caring for the MaineCare population at the end of life has proven to be accurate with MaineCare hospice patients accessing care at the very end of life when the intensity of hospice care is significant - nursing care, complex pharmaceutical management for pain and anxiety, medical equipment in the home and intensive social work support to help the family navigate the pending death. All of this care is provided in a short period, sometimes just a few days or a week. This is why the legislature set a clear expectation that MaineCare reimbursement for hospice care needed to be higher than Medicare hospice rates of payment.
Thank you,
Sara Ratcliffe Executive Director Home Care & Hospice Alliance of Maine Sara@FrontlineCo.com

Currently, the HIE contains health records for more than 2.2 million individuals (both in-state and out-of-state residents), which are
made available to over 8,500 healthcare clinicians and staff to help improve the safety, quality, and

10032687:
Senator Margaret Rotundo, Chair Representative Drew Gattine, Chair Members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee
Senator Henry Ingewersen, Chair Representative Michele Meyer, Chair Members of the Health and Human Services Committee
RE: Testimony IN OPPOSITION - LD 210, Language Part "SS" Establishes a $0.70 cents per pharmacy prescription assessment on pharmacy providers
Dear Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, and Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services Committee:
My name is Steve Maki and I am a Pharmacist and Owner of Spruce Mountain Pharmacy in Jay. I have been practicing pharmacy for almost 30 years. I have spent the last 15 years at Spruce Mountain Pharmacy an independent community pharmacy. I am submitting testimony in opposition of LD 210 part SS which establishes a $0.70 cent per pharmacy prescription assessment on pharmacy providers. Unfortunately, due to staffing limitations, I am not able to be at the committee hearing today. It is my hope through this written testimony will convey the passion I have for my community pharmacy and communities we service will not go unnoticed. The proposed tax assessment of $0.70 per prescription will have a negative impact upon my pharmacy and other community pharmacies across the state. Here are some of the key points I feel the Committees must understand and carefully consider during this process. First, Governor Mills Administration is saying this will be budget neutral in aggregate but there is no guarantee that individual pharmacies will be made whole. This language is a RED FLAG to me as a business owner. There is no doubt in my mind there will be winners and losers. Everyone is taxed at the same rate per prescription, but only pharmacies that fill a high degree of MaineCare prescriptions will have any chance to be made whole. This is NOT PHARMACY NEUTRAL as the Administration claims. Pharmacies that have a high elderly population stand to lose, as Medicare Part D dispense fees will not be increased. My independent community

pharmacy will pay the tax and potentially not received any additional payment(s) for the services provided to MaineCare patients. This is why I am opposed this tax increase.
Second, the tax and increased MaineCare dispense fee are two different initiatives, and only the $0.70 tax is in the budget. We've been told they will be linked together, but I have significant concerns that one might move forward without the other. How do we know we will both get both passed? What is our recourse if only the tax increase passes? Can we rescind the tax if the increase MaineCare reimbursement doesn't move forward? Given the uncertainty with federal funding, there is no guarantee the federal draw down of funds will materialize. You are asking me to trust my business to a promise you may not be able to keep. This is why I am opposed this tax increase.
Third, it has been well-documented that pharmacies are struggling in Maine and across the country and looking for transparency, with fair and reasonable reimbursements for the prescriptions and pharmaceutical care we provide. I have grave concerns that Maine pharmacies will close if this initiative passes. This will not just negatively affect independent pharmacies. It is well-documented that chains are also closing across the country. With the closing of pharmacies, we are sacrificing patient care. We are losing 10 or more pharmacies a day nationwide. There are not enough pharmacies to fill the gaps we're seeing. I have not seen any information about how the administration is going to collect the $0.70 tax on out of state mail order pharmacies under the proposal. Adding a new disadvantage my pharmacy will have to contend with while trying to compete with nationally owned Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBM's) mail-order pharmacies. This is why I am opposed this tax increase.
Fourth, Governor Mills budget proposal is anticipating significant increased spending. Pharmacists don't determine who qualifies or not for MaineCare. Why are we funding this on the back of pharmacies when the state has said they cannot "hold harmless" pharmacies with this scheme? We do not have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem. We need to address the root cause and get spending under control. How many more business need to close due to high tax burden and government mandated expenses before we get spending under control. This is why I am opposed this tax increase.
Finally, based on my numbers from 2024 a $0.70 tax per prescription would take another $36,400.00 out of my business. What does this mean to a small business like Spruce Mountain Pharmacy?
1. Reduction in Profitability: I will have less money to reinvest or expand the business to provide new programs or services for our patients and community. This could stop new or replacement equipment purchases. This could have a negative impact on business growth going forward.
2. Raise prices on other goods: The reality is I cannot raise more revenue on prescriptions billed to insurances, with the reimbursement rates set by PBM contracts a/k/a MAC (maximum allowable cost) pricing and the Point-of-Sale collection of direct and indirect

remuneration (DIR) fees crushing reimbursements to the pharmacies we can not pass this new tax along to the consumer. I could raise the prices on non-insurance bill prescriptions but when this is less than 10% of my business it's hard to make up $36,400.00. This will drive inflation in the pharmacy business sector into the over-the-counter medications and other nonprescription cost. Or we will have to stop customer focused care as we cut back on what we can offer to our patients (your constituents).
3. Hiring and Wage Impact: the loss in profit will force me to limit staff development, force a hiring freeze, not allow me to offer competitive wages for new staff, not allow for the expansion of employee benefits or worse a reduction of benefits and delay raises and bonuses.
As the past president of the Maine Pharmacy Association, I had the opportunity to travel across the state and speak with owners, pharmacist, pharmacy technicians, support staff and customers. The level of pharmaceutical care being provided to our citizens by our community pharmacies was inspiring to say the least. We are here to provide people to have quicker access to their medication. We are filling prescriptions and offering education on getting the best use from the prescription medication to achieve positive health outcomes. We are selling and giving advise to customers on over-the-counter medications. We are one of America's most trusted and easily accessible healthcare professionals. We stepped up during the COVID crisis to vaccinate and continue to provide pharmaceutical care as an essential business in the state. We offer health screening through, diabetes education, blood pressure checks and medication reviews. Medication management to support our customers with adherence, compliance packaging and education to help patients with complex medication regiments. Pharmacies provide medical equipment and supplies like mobility aids, blood pressure monitors, pulse oximeters, wound care, diabetes testing equipment etc. Community pharmacies serve as an accessible healthcare hub to their community, often without an appointment. The pharmacies offer convenient, patient centered care to their community. If community pharmacies close who is going to fill in the void?
I appreciate the time and attention you are giving this proposed tax assessment of $0.70 per prescription. I hope I have provided some insight to the negative impact this tax would have on the citizens of Maine.
Respectfully submitted,
Steve Maki, RPH
Spruce Mountain Pharmacy
Jay, ME 04239

10032616:
COR Health Services Testimony on LD 210, the Governor's proposed Biennial Budget
February 12, 2025
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Appropriations & Financial Affairs Committee and Health & Human Services Committee:
My name is Tammy Polakowski, and I serve as RN and ADON/Northern Region for COR Health Service. I am submitting testimony in opposition to LD 210, the Governor's Biennial Budget proposal.
Specifically, I am concerned about the lack of funding for MaineCare rate increases for home care service and the lack of funding for MaineCare cost-of-living adjustments.
I feel as though I am in a unique position, having worked as a field nurse as well as Nurse Coordinator and Assistant Director of nursing. I am also an Alliance member. As a field nurse, I have worked with medically fragile, complex medical, and chronic conditions in the pediatric population which we serve. These conditions require ongoing medical monitoring, treatment, and support to the families. Without proper care, they are at risk for future illness and complications. The parents must provide routine care, medication administration, and travel to appointments. This can have a huge impact on the family. There is emotional and financial strain, and a decline in physical health of the parent. The risk is even higher in single parent homes. I carry a caseload in Northern Maine and frequently visit the homes of these pediatric clients. I hear of the struggles they have when they are not able to obtain in home nursing. Most of the parents are unable to work due to needing to be home to care for their sick child. This takes away any financial security they may have had. This can certainly have a domino effect on the State of Maine's economy with these parents needing to access other state programs. Not having nursing in the home can also put a strain on PCP offices, urgent care and emergency Depts, and inpatient facilities. Home care is clearly the most cost effective as well as the safest for these clients. Inpatient stays after surgical procedures are drastically reduced when there is nursing in the home.
There is an urgent need for RN staffing in the State of Maine. We are unable to offer a pay rate that can compete with inpatient facilities. The reimbursement rates that we have are outdated and simply not enough to hire staff for the large amount of unstaffed hours we have. I urge you to consider MaineCare rate increases for home health services in Maine, specifically pediatric in home nursing. Without the rate increases we will be unable to hire nurses that are much needed across the state. For the nurses we have on staff, without the COLA that we were expecting, we will be unable to retain the

staff we have due to only being able to offer minimal annual pay increases. It is much appreciated that the proposed budget has an investment that stabilizes the Mainecare program, but in order for homecare services in the State of Maine to move forward, it is crucial that rate increases and COLA are included in the biennial budget
Thank you, Tammy Polakowski RN ADON/Northern Region COR Health Services TPolakowski@corhealthservices.com (207)210-1295

Testimony of Velia Janerico-Matthews, resident of Skowhegan, ME
LD 210: An Act Making Unified Appropriations and Allocations for the Expenditures of State Government, General Fund and Other Funds, and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30,
2025, June 30, 2026, and June 30, 2027
February 12, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of both the Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services Committees.
I am writing this letter to express my concerns over the Governor's biennial budget and the fact that it does not include any form of cost of living raises (COLAs) for the next two years. While these lack of raises may seem insignificant to some, I can assure you, that they can have a significant impact on those of us who dedicate over the average 40 hours to our work. It is important to acknowledge that our current economy is not one that people live in with ease. It presents many challenges for many workers as they strive to maintain their standard of living in the face of rising inflation. In the past, a wage of $16 dollars per hour was considered fair and sufficient for basic needs, but the current economic climate has led to the realization that this amount does not adequately cover living expenses.
I work in a field where people rely on me daily for support. I assist individuals in achieving independence, provide transportation, offer personal care, and support goal setting and achievement. Every day, they rely on me to be their advocate, to be a beacon of support and someone they can always count on. And it's not just me they rely on, but the entire staff of the company I work for.
However, we have encountered a challenge in our efforts to maintain a sufficient staff. It is unfortunate that individuals are not applying to join our team, and those who do join often do not remain with us for an extended period. I believe this is not due to any shortcomings on our part, but rather, I feel, it may be due to the competitive nature of the wages offered by other companies in the area. Testimony of Wanda Pelkey CEO, First Atlantic HealthCare
Wednesday, February 12, 2025 at 1:00 PM
To the Joint Standing Committeeon Appropriations and Financial Affairs and the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
In Opposition to:
LD 210, An Act Making Unified Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending
June 30, 2025, June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027
Good afternoon, Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Senator Ingwerson, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committees. My name is Wanda Pelkey and I serve as the CEO of First Atlantic Healthcare. I am providing this written testimony in opposition of LD 210.
Our company represents 20 nursing and residential care facilities throughout Maine, caring for about 1,400 of our State's frailest citizens. Over the last few years our First Atlantic group sadly lost three nursing facilities due to MaineCare rates being too low to cover the high cost of labor. Our facility losses, like the others in Maine, are dispersed throughout the state which underscores the underfunding problem isn't limited to a certain region or rural vs urban. I know all too well the pain and suffering each closure brings to residents and their families, including some who were forced to move multiple times due to sequential closures.
Thus, I'm grateful the legislature took these closures seriously and last year appropriated funding for Nursing Facility Rate Reform so reimbursements could better fund the cost of care and halt closures. I appreciate the collaboration by DHHS and providers to develop the new rates which were implemented on January 1. In fact, the system is so new that we haven't yet received our first payments under the new rates. Yet already, there are elements proposed in Part UU of LD 210 that will impact rates and jeopardize the survival of our long term care homes.
First and foremost, the LD proposes to strip away annual cost of living increases (COLA) that are vitally necessary for both nursing and residential care facilities to provide competitive wages and benefits to our direct care workers.
Many other provisions relate specifically to the new Nursing Facility Rate Reform system:  LD 210 strips away every two-year rebasing in current statute and inserts language that requires rates get re-evaluated once every five years going forward. Because of

economic pressures driven by direct care worker shortages, rates should be reviewed more often to ensure they continue to support the cost of adequate staffing.  The bill also strips away funding language in the current statute that provides a regional wage adjustment so direct care rates are adjusted relative to hourly labor rate differences across Maine. Treating all regions in Maine the same ignores the reality of much higher cost of housing in southern Maine and higher wage rates needed by employees to live there.  LD 210 further jeopardizes the recent inclusion in statute that MaineCare rates must be high enough to pay all caregivers at least 125% of minimum wage. This was deemed vitally important by the Long Term Care Workforce Commission, and in 2021 the legislature enacted a measure to require the labor portion of the MaineCare reimbursement rate for all direct care workers to be set at 125% of the state minimum wage to attract and retain direct care workers for our growing health care needs. Making this requirement optional and subject to sufficient appropriations means rates will no longer be required to be adjusted when the minimum wage rate rises. Without this guarantee, facilities will no longer be able to afford the higher rates needed to attract CNAs who are the backbone of our workforce.
I appreciate your attention, and my apologies that I'm unable to be there in person to present testimony today. Please do not hesitate to contact me if you'd like to learn more about how this bill could endanger access to long term care services in Maine. Thank you.

THURSDAY, February 13, 2025, 10 A.M.
Chairs Rotundo, Ingwersen, Gattine and Meyer, and distinguished members of both the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and the Health and Human Services Committee, I am Bethany Sproul-Lebrun, Director of Childcare for the City of Augusta.
I offer my testimony in opposition to the proposed childcare cuts in the Governor's biennial budget draft. I urge you to carefully consider the far-reaching consequences these cuts could have on childcare providers, particularly the reductions to the wage supplement and the childcare scholarship program for childcare workers' children. These cuts would have serious consequences for both childcare providers and the families we serve.
Our program has proudly served the Augusta community for nearly 30 years, providing yearround care for school-aged children through before and after school programs, school vacations, snow days, and summer camps. Our motto has always been "When school is out, Childcare is in". This is an absolute essential service for the working parents and guardians of Augusta.
Currently, while we meet the required staffing ratios, we lack the additional staff needed to cover absences or to expand our enrollment. If we were able to hire just three more staff members, we could serve an additional 15-18 children, bringing our total enrollment to approximately 155-- about 55% of the student population of Hussey Elementary School. This decision is not only shortsighted but also detrimental to the well-being of Maine's children, families, and the future of our state. The facts are clear: Maine ranks 50th in the nation for education, according to recent assessments. Our students consistently underperform in key areas such as reading, math, and science proficiency. This is not a problem that begins in elementary school--it starts in the earliest years of a child's life. Research unequivocally demonstrates that access to quality early childhood education is one of the most effective ways to close achievement gaps and prepare children for success in school and beyond. By cutting funding to child care programs and staff, you are dismantling the very infrastructure that supports early learning and development, further exacerbating Maine's educational crisis.
Child care is not merely a convenience for working families; it is a vital component of a child's cognitive, social, and emotional development. Studies show that children who participate in high-quality early learning programs are: - More likely to read at grade level by third grade, a key predictor of future academic success. - Less likely to require special education services or repeat grades, reducing long-term costs for the state. - More likely to graduate high school and pursue higher education or meaningful employment, contributing to Maine's economic vitality.
The proposed cut will have devastating consequences. It will force child care centers to close, reduce the availability of affordable care, and leave thousands of families without access to the early learning opportunities their children desperately need. This will disproportionately impact low-income families, widening the gap between Maine's most vulnerable children and their peers.

At a time when Maine should be investing in its future, this cut represents a step backward. It undermines the progress we have made and sends a message that our children's futures are not a priority. How can we expect to improve our education system when we are actively dismantling the programs that prepare children to succeed in school?
I urge you to reconsider this decision and prioritize the well-being of Maine's children. Restore the $15 million in child care funding and commit to strengthening early childhood education programs. Our children deserve nothing less than a strong start in life, and our state's future depends on it.

10032965:
February 13, 2025
Dear Senator Rotundo, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Meyer and esteemed members of the Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services:
My name is Cait Vaughan, and I am testifying on behalf of my employer, Grandmothers for Reproductive Rights (GRR!). Ours is an established grassroots organization with more than 500 Maine-based members, focused on securing more just and healthy lives for future generations, by educating, organizing, and advocating intergenerationally. The Reproductive Justice movement--founded in 1994 by twelve Black American women activists--outlines three tenets to their bold human rights framework. These include: the human rights to have children, to not have children, and to raise the families we do have in safe, healthy, and sustainable communities. It is this last core principle that brings GRR! here today in solidarity with immigrant Mainers whose well-being, opportunities for health, and lifelong potential are threatened by proposed cuts to SNAP and TANF.
I remember when Governor LePage was in office and many of us were pushing back on attempts to slash benefits for immigrant members of Maine's communities. It is frankly heartbreaking and shameful that we are here again--not just living under a federal administration determined to scapegoat and target immigrants for exclusion and removal--but confronting a Democratic governor's budget proposal that suggests finding "savings" by making cuts to social safety net programs. It is not possible to encourage young adults and families to settle, learn, work, pray, create, research, recreate, and innovate in Maine if we deny their humanity. What other message are we sending, if we move food, basic cash assistance, and workforce development programs out of reach for the most vulnerable families and individuals?
I recently supported a birth, as a doula, alongside a newly arrived, asylum-seeking woman from Congo. Only in the country a few months, she was sleeping on a mat at the YMCA shelter with her husband and young child. On the day of her labor induction, this pregnant mother had not eaten a single meal all day. This is under the current regulations for SNAP and TANF, mind you. About to embark on the hardest task a human body can perform--childbirth--she was hungry and exhausted beyond belief from months of barely getting by. Yet, life will out, and she gave birth to a healthy and precious baby boy who knows only Maine as his first, and perhaps forever, home.
The frame of Reproductive Justice, as well as my own lived experience of living in childhood poverty and accompanying those in poverty through major life transitions, leads me to the conclusion that no humane government removes access to basic needs like food to balance a budget. I do not believe that any of you

believes an immigrant child is less deserving of nutrition and clean diapers than any other child. I trust you will reject the proposed cuts accordingly.
A budget is a moral document. I have been proud of our state because we fought in the recent past to expand access to social safety net programs so that people who have survived displacement, persecution, and violence are able to land here and begin anew. Immigrants are participating prominently in many industries, including direct care professions, like support services for disabled and older Mainers, which makes it possible for families of all formations and Mainers of all abilities to thrive. These same people are starting and expanding their families here in Maine, sowing the seeds of a vibrant and multicultural future for the entire state.
I know that tough decisions are ahead of you this budget season. I believe your moral compasses and creative determination will lead you to identify far better methods for securing savings and revenuegenerating sources. I, and Grandmothers for Reproductive Rights, strongly urge you to reject the proposal in Language Part VV of LD 210, which would repeal the unemployment hardship exception for statefunded SNAP and TANF benefits. All people making a life in Maine deserve to have their basic needs met and a fair shot at a healthy life; let's make it so.
Thank you for your time and consideration,
Cait Vaughan Director of Programs & Outreach Grandmothers for Reproductive Rights (GRR!)

Maine State Legislature Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs 5 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333-0005
Subject: Written Testimony to the Maine Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs - LD210 (Part A) Public Hearing on February 13, 2025
Dear Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, and Honorable Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs,
Thank you for the opportunity to provide written testimony to the State of Maine Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs to be included in the Public Hearing on the state budget proposal to cut $20 Million in childcare funding, on Thursday February 13th.
I am one of your constituents in Cape Elizabeth, and the founder and co-owner of a Maine business, Colby Company Engineering, located in Portland. I am writing to urge you to oppose the proposed budget cuts to child care in Maine. Governor Mills' biennial budget includes over $20 million in reductions that will harm families, child care educators, and Maine's workforce. These cuts include:
1. A $15 million annual cut to the Child Care Educator Salary Supplement Program, which would lower already low wages for child care professionals. (LD210, Section A-302)
2. The complete elimination of the Child Care Employment Award, making it harder for child care workers to afford care for their own children. (LD210, Section A-302)
3. A $3.6 million annual reduction in Head Start funding, limiting access to critical early learning programs for Maine's most vulnerable families. (LD210, Section A-331)
Maine is already facing a child care crisis with a lack of child care supply and affordability, and povertylevel wages for daycare staff. These proposed cuts will destroy an already fragile framework: forcing early childhood educators out of the workforce due to perilously low wages, coupled with their inability to afford or access child care for their own children, resulting in the loss of affordable child care for Maine families. Head Start is a critical program that provides important educational programming and child care to Maine families who may not otherwise have access to early education programs and resources. A loss of child care availability hurts all Maine families.
Maine's Permanent Commission on the Status of Women (PCSW) advises the Governor and the Maine Legislature about policy and social issues affecting women in the state of Maine. PCSW published a white paper, "Maine Needs Quality Affordable Childcare" in January 2024, it summarizes the importance of access to childcare, some of the current challenges this industry faces, and potential solutions to Maine's child care crisis. The number of child care providers in Maine has declined by 39% (from 1,134 to 702) since 2013. When child care is costly or unavailable where parents of young children live or work, they cannot work. As PCSW states in the White Paper: "The high cost of child care drives women out of the workforce at a time when employers all over the state are desperate for workers." Not only does the lack of availability and affordability of child care hurt Mainers now, it also impacts our future. "Quality childcare prepares children to succeed in school and eventually, the workplace...The Brookings Institute conducted a longitudinal study of children who had received early care services across income levels. This study found that children from low-income homes who had received 24 months or more of high-quality early childhood education in their first five years were more

likely to graduate from college, and had higher salaries at age 26. High quality child care is a long-term investment that helps break the cycle of intergenerational poverty."
Maine's early childhood educators are in the bottom 3% of wage earners, many struggling to make ends meet and live paycheck to paycheck. The loss of the Child Care Educator Salary Supplement Program will tip that balance making educators unable to remain in this critical workforce, forcing them to leave this field to earn higher paying wages. Child care centers across Maine already struggle to retain and hire enough staff. When parents cannot find affordable child care, they cannot work, and businesses like mine cannot find employees, and our economy suffers. ReadyNation issued a recent report that found that child care shortages cost Maine's economy $403 million per year, more than double the estimated impact in 2019. Our Maine business has a staff of 70 people, 23% of our staff have children requiring full time or part time child care, which enables these staff to be a part of our workforce. Maine child care spots would decrease due to the impact of these budget cuts, and this would negatively impact my company's ability to adequately staff our office, and hurt Maine families who rely on child care.
As an employer, I can tell you that hiring professional engineers and architects should really only take between 3 to 6 months. For the past 5 years, it has taken between 8 and 14 months to hire new employees. Most of them are now coming via a recruiter which costs many thousands of dollars, and they are coming from out of state. The majority of our interviews with these folks include conversations about a lack of affordable housing and the cost of child care. As of late, we have started to see some relief in the housing market, but there has been no relief in the child care area, and these budget cuts would only make it worse.
Colby Co. has had the pleasure of partnering with the United Way of Southern Maine (UWSM) as they develop an independent non-profit organization called United 4 Child Care (U4CC). Through U4CC, UWSM is creating a new community-based model for daycare: identifying vacant commercial spaces; coordinating with building owners and local businesses who need and want to assist their staff with obtaining daycare; collaborating with child care experts and providers to create operations and business plans to open new non-profit daycare centers in southern Maine. CCE has been working closely with UWSM to evaluate several buildings in Cumberland and York counties, to assess spaces for renovations to convert each site into new daycare centers. U4CC is convening local businesses to collaborate and contribute financially to the start-up and operational costs for new daycare centers, creating new daycare seats that will be made available to those businesses' employees. Through this community collaboration, U4CC is working to solve this critical need in Maine: lack of child care supply and affordability, and poverty-level wages for daycare staff. Part of the U4CC program includes a workforce development component to not only train and educate daycare staff to become high quality early childhood educators, but also to teach these staff about the operational side of running a new daycare business, to create a sustainable model to attract and retain educators to serve an urgent problem in Maine.
I ask you to advocate for a budget that invests in child care affordability, educator wages, and infrastructure so our communities and economy can thrive. I appreciate your time and urge you to oppose these harmful budget cuts, to support Maine's working families. Please do not hesitate to contact me if you would like to discuss this important issue further, and thank you for your service to the State of Maine.
Sincerely,

Calen B. Colby, P.E. Colby Co. Engineering 207.553.7753 (Main)

Dear HHS Committee,
I am writing to express urgent concern over the proposed cuts to Maine's child care investments in the biennial budget, which threaten the stability of an already fragile industry. These cuts would have significant, far-reaching consequences for child care educators, families, and the state's future prosperity. I'm asking you to stand up for your community child care programs and its predominantly woman-led workforce and small business owners and oppose these cuts.
As a parent of a daycare-age child, I know that many of the educators at my child's daycare have worked in the field for 10+ years. They are taking care of the most precious things in our lives - our children. These children are in the most crucial stage of their development and these teachers are responsible for giving them their all - and they deserve to be treated that way. They love the work they do and this field is so important to building the future we all want and deserve. The impact of early childhood education, and specifically head start are far reaching and long term. Early learning provides children with a `head start'. Research shows children are more ready for kindergarten, future success in school and later in life. Children who attend Head Start are less likely to end up incarcerated, further costing the state and taxpayers down the road. Virtually ending the cycle of poverty.
While Head Start may receive funding from the federal government, it's not enough. Maine should be proud to be one of the only states who supports Head Start funding and not using it as a reason to provide less.
I understand cuts are needed, but these are too deep and across the board. Cutting the wage supplement in half, the head start support in half is too deep. This will have detrimental, long term, and major impacts on the children in Maine. Families can't work if children don't have high quality childcare. As you heard through many testimonies- early childhood care is vital in Maine. Did you know that Head Start programs also provide childcare?
Please reconsider these deep and multiple cuts that will have dire impacts on the working families of Maine.
Maine's Child Care Educator Salary Supplement Program The Governor's proposed $15 million annual cut to child care educator wages would be devastating. Currently, educators earn an average of $16.40 per hour (around $34,000 annually), insufficient for supporting a family. Reducing the wage by half would lower it to $15.15 per hour ($31,500 annually), worsening financial strain and exacerbating workforce shortages. This program has seen an 11% increase in educators since its inception, yet cutting funding now would reverse these gains and harm the industry's progress.
Maine's Child Care Employment Award The child care tuition assistance program, which was delayed over a year in its implementation, is crucial for recruiting and retaining staff by helping workers cover child care costs. The funds were exhausted within three months, supporting around 400 professionals, with over 450 still on the waiting list. This program is vital for maintaining a stable workforce and improving child care quality statewide. The year-long delay already deprived educators of essential savings on their child care costs, and cutting the program now would significantly disrupt the support they are receiving.

Head Start Maine's $3.6 million investment in Head Start serves 1,742 low-income children. Eliminating this funding would result in the loss of services for 180 children, the closure of 9 classrooms, and potential loss of millions in federal funding. This is a direct threat to the education and well-being of Maine's most systemically vulnerable children.
Conclusion Cuts to these essential programs would result in over $4,000 in lost wages for child care educators, the removal of 400 professionals from the tuition assistance program, and the loss of critical services for 180 children. These cuts undermine the entire early care and education system and threaten Maine's long-term economic growth. Now is the time to invest in our child care workforce and ensure a stable future for Maine's children and families.
Thank you for your attention to this crucial issue.
Regards,
Austin Sims 325.864.6094 Portland

Senator Rotundo, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Gattine, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee, My Name is Deborah Hagler. I have practiced pediatrics in Maine for 27 years. I reside in Harpswell, Maine. I cochair the Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics Committee on Healthy Mental
Development. Thank you for hearing testimony from the Maine AAP Chapter.
It is during the 3rd trimester that the brain loses its smooth appearance and begins to take on the characteristic folds that produce the very recognizable landmarks of the human brain. At the microscopic level connections ( called synapses) are being established between nerve cells at an approximate rate of 700 new synapses per second. By birth the average brain weighs about 350-400 grams1 and is growing gangbusters- most rapidly in the first 2 years such that by kindergarten the human brain is about 90% of its adult size.1,2 Early experiences fuel the formations of neuronal connections, growth, and are critical for the development of the human brain.3 Over the last several decades research has discovered many of the key details of this undertaking and the importance environmental factors in this process from the role of a loving enriching environment to the challenges presented by infections, nutritional deficiencies environmental neglect, and various forms of childhood trauma.
Childhood trauma exposes the developing brain to elevated levels of the stress hormone cortisol which changes production of microRNA altering production of cellular proteins in the brain and prevents the addition of chemical groups to proteins on DNA preventing the production of proteins.3,4 Chronic neglect decreases input into the system that enhances the functional and structural development of the brain. Data from the Bucharest Early Intervention Project studied and followed infants and toddlers for a 12-year period that had randomly been assigned to foster care or to remain in institutional care at different time periods in their developmental trajectory. Using PET Scans, MRI scans and EEG testing changes in brain functioning and structure overtime were demonstrated. Children remaining in institutional care ( a proxy for environmental neglect) showed reductions in metabolism in areas that were critical for emotional control and cognitive functioning and brain imaging studies showed an overall decrease in brain volume in those raised in an institutional environment.5 This study also demonstrated subsequent changes or "recovery" to more normalized structure and function when children were placed into an adoptive or foster care setting- highlighting the profound plasticity of the developing brain. The earlier the intervention the better the recovery. Timing matters. 5,6
Children growing up exposed to toxic stress or in under-resourced environments can begin school with significant disadvantages in language use, vocabulary, emotional regulation and executive function and the research shows that this can be mitigated by providing good quality childcare programs and resources.4 Nobel prize winning economist Dr. James Heckman has studied the economics of early childhood extensively. Estimates for every dollar invested in early childhood programming can yield from 4-9 dollars in return. 7 The Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics is opposed to cuts that would decrease access to HeadStart and diminish funding to attract a well-trained qualified child educator workforce. A Harvard neuroscientist said our nature needs nurture. Maine and its

children need and deserve access to the most robust early childhood system of support for their
development and all our futures.

Chairs Rotundo, Ingwersen, Gattine and Meyer, and distinguished members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services Committees, I am Brigadier General Dwaine Drummond. U.S. Army (retired) and I offer this testimony in opposition to the Governor's proposed budget cuts in child care and Head Start programs.
I served more than 36 years in the Army and Maine National Guard, commanding at the company, battalion, and brigade levels. I am also a member of the organization Mission: Readiness, which advocates for state and federal programs that lead to better outcomes for our kids, reduce crime, strengthen national security, and builds a better workforce. Maine Mission: Readiness is 25 retired admirals and generals who champion research-supported solutions that help keep kids healthy, welleducated, and out of trouble, so that they can pursue whatever path they want in life, including military service, if they so choose. In addition, I am a father and former middle school coach. I have a personal stake in advocating for programs that help kids be successful in school and give them greater opportunities as adults. My Mission: Readiness colleagues and I are concerned about the dire need to prepare our children for their future and that preparation starts in their youngest years.
Some might wonder how a crisis-level lack of high-quality, affordable early care and education could impact our national security. The U.S. Department of Defense's ineligibility rate is strong evidence of the need to do more, earlier.
Unfortunately, 77% of America's 17- to 24-year-olds are not eligible to serve in the military, if that is their career choice. The reasons for ineligibility include lack of physical fitness, lack of educational attainment, substance abuse, and involvement in serious crime -- often drug-related.
Very often people think of our military in terms of the fast movers and high-tech systems: the F-35 Lightning 2 fighter jets, ships like the DDG 51 destroyers, the American M1A2 Abrams tanks, and other
482 Congress St., #303 / Portland, ME 04101 / 207-751-0506
EducateMaine.org

amazing state-of-the-art technologies. These weapons are essential, but even more essential are the people who stand ready to defend our country and carry out its mission. If 77% of young Americans are ineligible for military service, our nation risks not having qualified people needed to secure our future. This is not just a problem for the military; it impacts all career fields, all citizens.
Fortunately, we can address these disqualifiers with early intervention and support. A child's first five years are fundamental to the success or failure that comes afterwards. Young children develop core preliteracy and pre-math skills and build the foundations for all later cognitive learning and team building skills. That's why high-quality child care programs are so important.
Research shows that programs like high-quality public pre-K, child care, and Head Start can help create a stronger educational foundation, prevent obesity, and reduce behavioral issues. One study of the Perry Preschool Program found that almost half of the preschool graduates were performing at grade level by the age of 14, compared with just 15 percent of their peers who did not participate in the program. The kids who attended Perry Preschool were also 44% more likely to graduate from high school.
By providing more young children with high-quality child care opportunities for early learning, we can help them become successful students who are more likely to finish school and pursue any career path of their choice.
Cutting in half the state's support for wage stipends for our critical child care workforce is a move in the wrong direction. If implemented, this cut would result in an average reduction in hourly wage for child care educators by $1.25/hr. (from the current average of $16.40/hr. to $15.15/hr.) thus bringing the average median wage further away from that of other entry-level jobs. Who will we find to work in this critical field for those low wages?
If it's the state's priority to support our child care sector, which in turns supports working parents in every other sector of our economy, this cut will undermine the goal of Governor Mill's 10-year economic plan "to build worldclass child care in Maine."
Head Start programs across our state serve Maine's poorest and most at-risk children. Cutting $3.6 million annually in General Fund support for Head Start will only make this vital early learning and care program less available to the children who need it the most.
I was one of hundreds of citizens who publicly supported and encouraged the 2023 investments legislators made in child care and Head Start programs. I stand by my belief that such investments are worthy of your continued support.
EducateMaine.org

I encourage your committees to reject Governor's Mill's budget proposal to cut child care (as proposed on page A302) and Head Start (as proposed on page A331) programs in the biennial budget before you. Like all of you, members of Mission: Readiness want all young people in Maine and across our great nation to grow up to be citizen-ready in whatever field they seek -- to become our future workforce, our military leaders, our taxpayers, and our community, state, and national leaders. Helping to give our youngest citizens the foundations needed for later success is a wise investment of our state resources.
EducateMaine.org

Re: Testimony on the Governor's Budget Proposal and Child Care are Funding Cuts
Dear Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services Committee,
Thank you for the opportunity to testify regarding the governor's proposed budget and its impact on Child Care funding in Maine. My name is Ingrid Stanchfield, CEO of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Kennebec Valley, which provides Child Care for over 300 children at 3 Child Care locations; Gardiner, Chelsea and Palermo. More than 30 parents of these children work for the State of Maine. I am writing to express my deep concern over the proposed cuts to Child Care funding and to urge the Legislature to reconsider these reductions in the best interest of Maine's families, children, and the economy.
Child Care is a critical part of Maine's economy, enabling parents to participate fully in the workforce and contribute to the state's economic growth. Without reliable and affordable Child Care options, many workers--particularly women--may face significant barriers to employment, leading to reduced household income and lower productivity. Additionally, Child Care professionals themselves are crucial contributors to Maine's economy.
Child Care Professionals have counted on the monthly stipend to support their daily living expenses. I asked staff to share with me how important the State funded monthly bonus, and the coverage of weekly Child Care fees are to them. Here is just a piece of what they shared, and their full comments are in my printed testimony:
BGCKV Child Care Professional #1
"Without receiving free Child Care I also wouldn't be able to continue to work. On my salary I couldn't afford to pay $270 dollars a week for Child Care."
"I am dedicated to the field of Early Childhood Education. I went to school to get an associate's degree in early childhood. It is very unsettling to have to worry about how I would come up with enough money each month to pay my bills if my current Child Care benefits were not available."

BGCKV Child Care Professional #2
"When asked the question, "How important is the monthly Child Care stipend?", I am stopped in my tracks and left speechless for a moment. Most importantly, that stipend is a big portion of how I cover my family's health insurance. Not only am I a cardiac patient, but I also have a son who needs health care as well. Without that health insurance we of course wouldn't be able to receive care to remain healthy. That is just ONE of the MANY important reasons my family's lives depend on this."
"I am not sure how we would get by if I had to pay $250 a week for Child Care from my weekly income as a Child Care professional. When adding up the amount of free Child Care and the monthly stipend is, I begin to fret. I begin to feel uneasy about our day to day lives. How would we get by? How would we be able to feel comfortable with no money? I urge you to consider the many families that will be suffering with this possible change."
BGCKV Child Care Professional #3
The extra monthly bonus gives my family the ability to create memories. I'm not talking about trips or anything fancy. I'm talking about family dinners at the kitchen table, getting to say goodnight to my son, having the extra time to sit and talk to my husband and create plans and goals. The monthly bonus makes it, so I don't have to go out and get a second job. If I lose this Child Care bonus in my checks, not only am I going to face the fact that I might need to get a second job but then it will create fear. Fear I won't be able to help my son make daily improvements, fear I won't get to create memories with my husband in the time we have left together, fear I will not be the best version of myself out of exhaustion, fear that when the day comes to an end, I have nothing else to give.
My "job" and yes, I put it in parenthesis because my job is something I take huge pride in. The children in my care every day at Child Care are my children, the families are my families, my job is my home away from home. This is a place I go every day and let my walls down, help little minds grow, develop and become the next generation of our State of Maine.
"The monthly bonus has given me so much security and hope that I won't miss the precious moments in my life. I know that I am only one person, but I hope with reading how much this bonus affects just one person will help you understand how much it affects every Child Care professional in the State of Maine."
The Governor's proposed $15 million annual cut to Child Care educator wages is a direct threat to the stability of Child Care programs that are already facing critical issues with hiring and retaining qualified staff. If Child Care stipends were reduced by 50% that would be a decrease of $60,000 annually for the Child Care Professionals of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Kennebec Valley.

Cutting funding now would be a grave mistake, undermining efforts to build a stable, sustainable workforce and putting the future of our children at risk. It's time to prioritize the people who are shaping our future--our Child Care Professionals. Just the announcement of this funding cut has created uncertainty for Child Care Professionals working at the Boys & Girls Clubs of Kennebec Valley. It is very sad that young professionals can make a better annual income working in fast food service and retail than they can helping our youngest learners. Many of our Child Care Professionals are individuals who grew up at the Club and decided to continue their education in the Child Care field so they could give back to the next generation of Club kids growing up at the Club.
Additionally, programs like the Child Care Employment Award help retain and recruit Child Care employees by addressing the financial burdens they face. The tuition assistance program, which was designed to cover tuition costs for those working in licensed Child Care programs, demonstrated immediate demand, with funds exhausted within just three months, leaving several Boys & Girls Clubs of Kennebec Valley Child Care Professionals on the waiting list. Eliminating or reducing such programs will further destabilize an already struggling workforce. For the Boys & Girls Clubs of Kennebec Valley, eliminating the Child Care Employment Award would have an impact of $33,000 annually.
Instead of reducing Child Care funding, I urge the Legislature to invest in sustainable, long-term solutions that support working families and the Child Care workforce. Please consider maintaining and expanding educator stipends, increasing subsidies for lowincome families, implementing Child Care funding to organizations based on available slots and providing incentives for childcare workers to remain in the field.
Maine has an opportunity to lead in supporting working families and ensuring that every child has access to quality Child Care. I respectfully ask that you reconsider the proposed cuts and work toward a budget that prioritizes the well-being of our children and the strength of our workforce.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Ingrid Stanchfield CEO Boys & Girls Clubs of Kennebec Valley

EducateMaine.org

Those of us on the front line in the fight against crime understand that we will never fix the crime problem solely through arrests and imprisonment. We can save lives, hardship - and money - by investing in programs that can keep children from growing up to become criminals in the first place.
High-quality early learning programs are a great crime reduction strategy. This is backed up by a lot of research, including the 30-year study of the Chicago Child-Parents Centers and a more recent MIT study of the Boston preschool program.

Our program director advises that if the wage supplement is reduced, as proposed by the Governor, she knows she will lose dedicated and highly educated staff (all with teaching certifications and some even with masters' degrees). Chairs Rotundo, Ingwersen, Gattine and Meyer, and distinguished members of both the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and the Health and Human Services Committee, I am Jason Moen, Chief of Police in Auburn, Maine and President of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association. I am offering my testimony in opposition to the portion of the Governor's proposed biennial budget that seeks to reduce General Fund spending for child care and Head Start. Specifically, I oppose two cuts on page A-302 one proposes to reduce child care educators wage stipends by $15 million annually; and the second cut proposes the elimination of the program that helps low-paid child care educators cover the costs of child care for their own children. I also opposed the cut on page A-321, which proposes to reduce General Fund support to Maine's 11 regional Head Start programs by $3.6 million.
You might wonder why a police chief is interested in high-quality early learning taking place in Maine's child care and Head Start programs across our state. I believe, as do many other members of law enforcement, that prevention has got to be one of the weapons we use to fight crime in our cities and neighborhoods. Statistics show us that quality programs that help children get the right start in life reduce the chances of these children growing up and committing crimes.
As a member of Fight Crime: Invest in Kids, a crime prevention organization made up of 140 law enforcement members across Maine, I see the research that shows high-quality childhood programs, like child care and Head Start, are good investments to reduce the high cost of Maine's criminal justice system.
We know from this research, as well as from our own professional experiences, that a child who is successful in school is more likely to avoid brushes with the law as he or she grows up. Several studies show the connection between high-quality early education programs and long-term crime prevention.
482 Congress St., #303 / Portland, ME 04101 / 207-751-0506
EducateMaine.org

One study from Massachusetts Institute of Technology that was released just a year ago found that kids who had been through the Boston preschool program were less likely to be incarcerated in a juvenile facility during high school, compared to kids in Boston who hadn't been a part of the program.
In my own city of Auburn, we have seen encouraging results with our preschool programs. Students participating in Auburn's program achieved higher scores on the kindergarten screening assessment in comparison to students who were not enrolled.
According to Auburn's spring 2022 kindergarten screening data, the average score for students enrolled in Auburn's pre-K program was 85%, in comparison to 77% for students not enrolled. In addition, the 2022 Fall Northwest Evaluation Association assessment showed kindergarten students who had previously been enrolled in Auburn's pre-K program during the 2021-22 school year demonstrated proficiency levels of 99% in literacy and 95% in math.
High-quality child care and Head Start are the educational foundations that happen before public pre-K. To support the quality of programs we need more high-quality child care and Head Start across Maine, not less.
If the proposed wage cut to child care educators is adopted, then that would roll back the current average wage of $16.40/hr. (just over $34,000 annually) to $15.15/hr. (or $31,500 annually). WHO will work in child care for these low mages when they can earn more money in any retail or fast-food establishment? Such actions could well lead to the collapse of this vital sector of Maine's economy. As Auburn's Police Chief I can tell you that staff at our department do not have an option of working from home, or bringing their child/children to work with them. The same is true of other first responders, medical professionals, and so many other workplaces. Without child care parents cannot go to work.
With such low wages it is not surprising that Maine's new program to help child care workers pay for their own child care was so popular. It is one of the few workforce retention tools in child care. If anything, it should be enhanced, not eliminated.
The proposed Head Start cut of $3.6 million would result in 250 of Maine's poorest and most at-risk children losing their high-quality early learning programs.
The child care and Head Start educators in Auburn are some of our hardest workers I know, although many earn incredibly low wages for their efforts.
EducateMaine.org

That's why I ask each of you and your legislative colleagues to support Maine's child care and Head Start workforce by rejecting the proposed budget cuts to these vital programs. For me, the MRTQ stipend has a massive impact on my ability to stay in this profession and to advance my knowledge to support our states littlest learners. Testimony of Jocelyn Runnebaum before the Committee On Appropriations and Financial Affairs and the Committee on Health and Human Services in opposition to LD 210, the Governor's proposed Biennial Budget
February 11, 2025
Dear Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs,
My name is Jocelyn Runnebaum, I am a resident of Bath, Maine. I am here today to express my opposition to the Governor's proposed budget cuts to support to early childhood educator and Head Start programs. At a minimum, I urge you to reinstate funding for the following programs:
� Child Care Educator Salary Supplement - change from a proposed $15 million per year back to $30 million per year
� Child Care Employment Award - prevent elimination and return to the $2.5 million per year investment so childcare educators can pay for their own childcare
� Head Start Programs - add back $3.6 million per year to proposed budget cuts
I am a working mom striving to provide for my family's needs and to create opportunities for my son. My husband and I both need to work to provide for our family, especially since my husband is a Maine state employee with a salary known to be below market value. The influx of support through the Child Care Educator Salary Supplement and Child Care Employment Award programs have had tremendous impacts on my family. Before the introduction of these programs, our childcare was reduced from 5 days a week to 4 days a week because the childcare program we were in could not retain staff despite being a highly reputable program with national accreditation. In addition to the reduction in care, the provider also needed to increase the cost of care to be able to pay the early childcare educators a living wage. We were paying more money for less care, and I was not able to work as much as needed. Additionally, my son was not thriving in an environment he once was because of the constant turnover in staff who were leaving for better paying jobs. He came home emotional every day and nights were very hard on everyone in the family. This was an extremely challenging time for our family.
For the past two years, since the influx in financial support to childcare programs, my son has been thriving. This is not hyperbole. My son loves his teachers who are ever present, highly trained professionals providing more opportunities for learning than I ever could. We have not experienced provider turnover like we did before and my son comes home happy, full of stories about the adventures of his day, and raving about his teachers. I credit this to his teachers receiving better pay so they can afford to pursue their calling of early childhood education. I will note, his teachers still make much less than an early childhood educator should considering their critical role in keeping working families working. Working families like ours have reached the maximum of what we can afford for childcare. The influx of funding from the State is supporting the critical role childcare providers have in caring for our children AND keeping the economy afloat. This investment has been life-altering for my family. Simply put, if we had to pay more out of pocket for childcare, either my husband or I would have to drop out of the workforce. If you magnify that across other working families, the ripple effect would be a staggering blow to Maine's economy.
I understand the budget deficit is a very real challenge the state is currently facing. I urge the legislature to consider other ways to manage that challenge or find ways to increase funding for the state. Saving money at the expense of low- and middle-income Mainers by cutting critical programs is not the way to address this budget deficit.
Thank you,

Jocelyn Runnebaum

10035375:
Katie Morton Oxford SACC LD 210
Hello all, I am writing to you today to urge the state to reconsider their proposed budget cuts
to childcare. Having quality childcare in our state requires the support of our childhood educators, which includes childcare worker stipends and a budget for them to utilize for resources to care for our children. I have worked in healthcare for the last 17 years in Maine, always in rural communities. I have worked all shifts, and often working overtime and longer than expected shifts in order to care for said communities. I have cared for our most vulnerable; I worked on the frontlines in an emergency department throughout covid while pregnant with my son who just turned 4 years old yesterday. Without these incredible childhood educators, I would not be able to do my job. I know this to be true for many other healthcare professionals in the state as well. I can come to work and care for our communities while knowing that my son is getting quality care right down the street. His childcare center allows me to be a working mother and allows both myself and my husband to work which financially is a necessity for my family. It also allows my son not only to be cared for physically, but he is excelling developmentally because of the excellent curriculum his center provides. That curriculum and care would not be possible without appropriate funding. Childhood educators are worth their weight in gold; they are already not paid what they deserve, and budget cuts would only further create a deficit and would lead to loss of quality educators and needed childcare centers that allow people like me to continue to care for my community. Without them, there wouldn't be us. Nurses, doctors, CNAs, and all other professions that work tirelessly to serve our state; many would struggle if we lost our childhood educators and centers. Maine has an elderly population and one that has been rapidly decreasing due to the aging of our citizens. By cutting the budget of these necessary programs, you are discouraging young people from creating families and staying in our beautiful state. These children are our future and we should be protecting them and their resources at all costs. Thank you for your time.
10032992:
February 13, 2025
Written Testimony of Katie Rutherford, Executive Director of Frannie Peabody Center LD 210 - An Act Making Unified Appropriations and Allocations from the General Fund and Other Funds for the Expenditures of State Government and Changing Certain Provisions of the Law Necessary to the Proper Operations of State Government for the Fiscal Years Ending June 30,
2025, June 30, 2026, and June 30, 2027 Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committees on Appropriations and Financial Affairs and Health and Human Services, My name is Katie Rutherford and I am the Executive Director of Frannie Peabody Center, Maine's largest HIV/AIDS services organization. Our services include federally funded housing assistance in the form of rental subsides and short-term assistance; both of which fall short of meeting the high demand of housing needs among people living with HIV. I am writing in opposition to this budget initiative which limits access to housing assistance under the General Assistance Program, a service many of our clients rely on to achieve health and financial stability. Affordable housing has become more difficult to secure amid limited stock in addition to the sharp rise in cost of living. Individuals experiencing housing and financial instability, compounded by complex health conditions, need resources that far exceed the limitations and barriers presented by this budget initiative. The expectation that people experiencing poverty while grappling with a myriad of challenges including access to childcare, employment, healthcare, food security, and transportation, will be able to find relief with housing assistance capped at just three months is unrealistic and risks pushing families deeper into poverty. As subsidy waitlists continue to grow, and shelter capacity is limited, the consequences would be devastating. Obtaining and maintaining stable housing and the `housing-first' model is a crucial component of overall health for all Mainers. Preserving GA administrators' flexibility to meet the basic needs of people in Maine is both rooted in compassion and fiscally responsible. We urge you to oppose this portion of the budget. General assistance provides a lifeline for preventing and responding to homelessness.
30 Danforth St. Suite 309, Portland, Maine 04101 � peabodycenter.org
